The post Gen Alpha is coming: what are three priorities for universities when resources are tight?   appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr Steve Briggs, Director of Learning, Teaching and Libraries at the University of Bedfordshire.

The start of a new academic year is often a time for reflection. This year, I anticipate that much reflective bandwidth will be dedicated to how to navigate the many challenges facing the higher education sector. For me, it is a little different.

In a few years my children will be making decisions about higher education, and I find myself reflecting on how their generation will be different from previous cohorts. More particularly, in a context where there is unprecedented pressure to cut costs and find efficiencies, what should institutions prioritise to position themselves best for the arrival of Generation Alpha?

Gen Alpha

Generation Alpha is generally defined as those born in the early 2010s through to the mid-2020s, meaning the first members of the generation are likely to begin university around the end of the 2020s.

Higher education institutions will already be at varied stages of preparedness for Gen Alpha students. Between now and 2030, there is a window of opportunity to refine policies, practices, services and infrastructure to position institutions to meet the expectations and needs of these future students. Given the significant financial challenges at many institutions, I suggest three priorities that should be possible without significant large-scale investment.

Priority 1: Changing academic practices

Course teams should be supported to reflect critically on the extent to which their existing teaching and learning methods and approaches will meet the needs of Gen Alpha learners. For example:

Blended learning – Gen Alpha have used virtual classrooms and digital learning environments throughout their schooling. As such, many Gen Alpha learners are familiar with blended learning approaches and may consider combinations of in-person and digital learning to be normal. I anticipate that this familiarity will translate into the expectation that blended and flexible learning will be standard practice when they enter university.

Gamification and game-based learning – These approaches are already familiar to Gen Alpha learners through school learning platforms, apps (such as those used to learn a new language) and gaming platforms. I suggest that universities will increasingly need to consider how appropriate aspects of gamification might be integrated into learning experiences. This might include increased usage of virtual badges, credentials and progress indicators.

Information consumption – Gen Alpha is the first generation to have grown up immersed in digital technologies, including smart devices. Digital content is routinely packaged in condensed formats that combine visuals, sound and text. As such more traditional learning resources may need to be made more accessible to Gen Alpha, whilst still supporting the development of independent and critical thinking skills required for higher education studies.

Supporting course teams to enact such changes could be made a priority for a centralised learning and teaching unit. This focus could frame the provision of future academic development opportunities.

Priority 2: Optimising existing systems

Existing university systems may already have the functionality that would support Gen Alpha learners. However, this may not be fully utilised. For instance:

Personalisation – Gen Alpha are accustomed to digital environments that can be customised to reflect personal preferences. Many digital platforms provide recommendations based on user preferences and behaviours. Such experiences will likely influence expectations of personalised learning in higher education. For instance, students may expect to be able to adapt learning materials to meet individual preferences, such as converting a lecture recording into personalised, bitesize learning materials or a podcast.

AI as basic infrastructure – By 2030, AI is likely to have become part of basic infrastructure underpinning many aspects of society. Universities will therefore need to consider how their systems and approaches can keep pace with how Gen Alpha uses AI. I anticipate that this will include the mainstream provision of AI-enabled virtual tutors, assessment chatbots and automated feedback systems. Many digital learning systems are developing AI functionality that will be made available under existing licence agreements. It is critical that institutions are quick to evaluate and, where appropriate, leverage such developments.

Learning Technologists would be able to work with course teams to review, and potentially to update existing approaches. Where required system developments are not forthcoming, institutions should seek to ensure they have representation on product user groups so that they can lobby for developments that will support their operations to be included in product roadmaps.

Priority 3: Strengthening preventative well-being support

The World Health Organisation estimates that 14.3 per cent of 10- to 19-year-olds globally experience mental health conditions, although many remain unreported and untreated. Mental health is a well-established priority for universities. Looking ahead, I anticipate that support will need to continue to be prioritised to meet the needs of Gen Alpha:

Global challenge – Since 2013, there have been multiple events that have had transformative impacts on society. These include the pandemic, geopolitical instability, climate events and technological advancement. Gen Alpha has therefore grown up in a period of significant and sustained change. These experiences may foster resilience, flexibility and social responsibility. Equally, living through periods of uncertainty and disruption may contribute to anxiety and other mental health challenges. Further, while technology is affording more opportunities for personalisation, it too may contribute to feeling less belonging and loneliness.

Social media ban – The social media ban for under-16s may significantly change how young people socialise in-person and online. The transition may be particularly disruptive for older members of Gen Alpha who previously relied on social media as a primary means of communication and social connection. Regardless of the outcomes, it will be critical that universities consider and respond to whatever changes emerge in social norms, peer-to-peer communication and how student belonging is fostered.

Careers – We are at the start of an AI revolution. This has the potential to transform the nature of work, particularly disrupting traditional ‘white-collar’ professions. Universities must ensure that students are empowered to navigate this context. This will particularly need consideration of how to support more fluid and non-linear approaches to career planning, potentially in contexts of limited job security and the emergence of jobs that do not yet exist. For some, future careers options and aspirations could be a significant source of stress and anxiety.

Given resourcing challenges are likely to persist and capacity to invest in student support may remain limited over the coming years, institutions should consider whether additional preventative measures could be built into courses so that student support teams have capacity to provide targeted support to those with the greatest needs.

Positioning for success

Delivering these priorities will require centralised services, course teams and students to work together to co-create learning approaches and the wider student experience. Whilst this should not require substantial resources, it will need to be factored into institutional strategy and workload planning. The priorities discussed are very much intended to be illustrative rather than exhaustive. It is my hope that the reflections will spark both further discussion and potentially debate.

title: Headteachers say families will struggle after another rise in school dinner prices
summary: The price of a school dinner in a primary school will have risen from £2.60 to £3.40 since the start of 2026.
full_text:
A headteacher said she believes "families are going to struggle" as the price of school dinners is to go up for the second year in a row.

The price of meals for pre-school, primary and special school pupils will go up by 30p, for post-primary pupils will they will rise by 15%. It follows an increase of just under 20% introduced by the Education Authority (EA) in January 2026.

Áine Leslie, principal of Malone Integrated College in Belfast, said this will put further pressure on families who are already worried about the cost of living crisis.

But the EA said that the amount parents would have to pay was still well below the average cost of producing a school meal, estimated at over £5.20.

The latest increase, which will come into effect in January, means that the price of a paid for school dinner in a primary school or special school, for instance, will have risen from £2.60 to £3.40 since the start of 2026.

Pupils eligible for free school meals will not be affected.

The rise in school dinner prices is not the only measure introduced by the EA in response to what they describe as "an exceptionally challenging financial position".

There will also be a change to some menus in schools, replacing baked desserts with cheaper alternatives.

At Malone Integrated College about 55% of pupils have free school meal entitlement and there are also a lot of parents who are on lower incomes.

When the prices of school meals increased earlier this year, Leslie said she remembers "sitting with the head of the cafeteria and heartbreakingly decide how much to put up each item".

"I think the cumulative effect of this will be immense, particularly families who have multiple children, both at a primary school and a post-primary school, and trying to make ends meet, it's going to become incredibly difficult," Leslie told BBC News NI.

"I can't imagine what it would be like for families trying to budget that moving forward, as well as planning for Christmas.

"I firmly believe families are going to struggle at Malone.

"I do believe that there will be some families and some young people who will be worried about the stigma attached to this, and won't voice their concerns and won't ask for help. And as an integrated school, that's really sad for us.

She added: "I think it's going to be quite cutthroat for families.

"Already, we have some of our children, particularly in junior school talking about Christmas and how they've had discussions with their families that things are going to be much more scaled down this Christmas, just with the general cost of living crisis.

"And then this is only going to amplify the situation even more for young people."

Leslie added that not having a healthy, balanced diet or going without food will be a "barrier to learning".

Christos Gaitatzis is the principal of Omagh High and described the increase of 15% on a school meal as "excessive".

"What is the price index at the moment – is it 3,4, 5%? I would imagine that would be the reasonable increase that you would put on anything, so they are going three times the value - to me it is unreasonable," he told BBC News NI

Close to 30% of pupils at his school are on free school meals.

"You would expect that the cost for a child every week, when a price of a meal is close to £5, we are talking about £20 a week, £100 a month – that's a significant cost for lunch," Gaitatzis said.

"So other measures have to be taken by the families in order to make savings, for example pack lunches – then would that diet be balanced?

"We're talking about a society where the importance of nutrition provided by schools has significant impact on your mental and physical health, so you effectively deter these families and children having these nutritious meals by putting the price up.

"Clearly this will have an overall future impact on the health of the kids."

Northern Ireland's commissioner for children and young people said he was ''flabbergasted" at the change.

Chris Quinn said what makes the move "particularly difficult to accept is that it comes shortly after schools were directed towards energy-saving guidance advising people who were cold to wear more clothes rather than turn up the thermostat".

"I strongly advised the Education Authority to remove that guidance and made clear that responsibility for financial pressures in education should not be transferred to children and families."

The commissioner added: "Children did not create the financial crisis in education and they should not be expected to pay the price for it.

"School meals are not a luxury. For many children they are an essential part of the school day, and these increases will hit hardest those families already struggling with the cost of living."

In a statement, the EA said that they "were being asked to deliver important services to children and young people with insufficient funding".

They said that they hoped to save £20m by introducing the measures on top of £30m saved this year.

They also said costs, such as providing energy for schools, continued to rise.

"These were difficult decisions which sought to balance our commitment to children and young people alongside the requirement to live within the funding allocated for the year," the EA said.

"We are also mindful of the pressures across all public services in NI and of the fact that any overspend this year may impact on next year's finances."

The Northern Ireland Executive has yet to agree a budget amid a dispute with the secretary of state about how Northern Ireland is funded.

title: 5 reports, 5 different conclusions about fairness in school funding
summary:
“And nationally, schools in predominantly nonwhite districts receive $23 billion less in annual funding than their heavily white counterparts, according to a 2019 analysis by EdBuild.”             — Nikole Hannah-Jones, The New York Times, Oct. 4, 2026 “Contrary to common narratives, high-poverty and predominantly non-white districts have spent about the same as or more per pupil […]

The post 5 reports, 5 different conclusions about fairness in school funding appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
“And nationally, schools in predominantly nonwhite districts receive $23 billion less in annual funding than their heavily white counterparts, according to a 2019 analysis by EdBuild.”

— Nikole Hannah-Jones, The New York Times, Oct. 4, 2026

“Contrary to common narratives, high-poverty and predominantly non-white districts have spent about the same as or more per pupil than their more advantaged counterparts for decades.”

— Sarah Reber, Brookings Institution, July 2026 (Updated Nov. 9, 2026*)

If you’re confused about whether America’s public schools are shortchanging poor children or spending less money educating Black, Hispanic and Native American children, I was too. At least five major reports on school funding released in the past decade have reached conflicting conclusions. Some say disadvantaged students get more money than their wealthier, whiter peers. Others find substantial spending gaps in the opposite direction.

Why the strikingly different conclusions? Some reports count federal dollars for education, while others exclude them, and some adjust the dollars for regional differences in salaries or other expenses.

The five school spending reports — from Brookings, EdBuild, the Urban Institute, EdTrust and the Education Law Center— all use slightly different methodologies. One dates back to 2017 while another was just released last month.

“The fact is that when you ask different questions, you get different answers by design,” said Zahava Stadler, the former policy director at EdBuild (an advocacy and research group that closed in June 2020) who now directs the education funding equity initiative at the left-leaning think tank New America. “We’re not using different calculators here.”

Stadler made these comments at an August webinar held by EdFund, a nonprofit organization, after a surprising Brookings report landed in July 2026. That report pushed back against the narrative that school funding is terribly unfair to low-income children and implied that school funding inequality had been fixed. EdFund, which collects and commissions school finance research, wanted to help policymakers sort through the conflicting narratives and I attended the event. I’ll do my best to disentangle it all for you.

Brookings economist Sarah Reber found that the poorest school districts (the dark blue quintile #5 in the chart below) receive the most money per pupil from all government sources. She found a similar pattern in districts with the highest concentrations of nonwhite students. The white inset bars show national spending without New York City, which spends unusually large sums per student.

Meanwhile, the group that Hannah-Jones cited, EdBuild, found the opposite in its 2019 analysis. The group’s bar chart shows that per-student spending is lower in both poor and nonwhite districts.

They’re all crunching real data. And no one is accusing anyone else of chicanery or bad math. So what’s going on?

1. Federal money changes the picture

The Brookings report counted all sources of school funding: local, state and federal. EdBuild, EdTrust and the Education Law Center, a legal advocacy organization, counted only local and state dollars.

That’s a big difference. The federal government provides more than $50 billion in school-related aid, including $18 billion in Title I funding for poor children, $15 billion for students with disabilities and $19 billion for school meals. When you count all that money in the per-pupil spending calculations, poor school districts come out ahead.

The Urban Institute makes these differences visible by layering the sources of school funding, local, state and federal, one at a time. Local funding, much of it raised through property taxes, favors wealthier districts.

The addition of state funding narrows the gap, although some states contribute more to poor districts than others do.

Add federal funding, and poor districts receive more per pupil, on average, in almost every state.

So why exclude federal money? Stadler, the former EdBuild policy director, said she wanted to answer a narrow question: Are states doing their job to ensure that poor districts and districts serving children of color get the resources they need? Including federal aid, she said, “obscures” whether states are doing their part.

Federal aid is supposed to supplement state and local funding, not replace it. If states rely on Washington to close funding gaps, “they’re passing the buck,” Stadler said.

Brookings’ Reber, meanwhile, wanted to count all the money available to educate children. She worried that EdBuild’s findings were being misinterpreted to mean disadvantaged children actually receive fewer dollars.

Both are answering legitimate questions. One measures state and local responsibilities; the other measures the total resources available to students.

2. Adjusting for regional cost differences

Brookings simply counts the dollars. EdBuild, EdTrust and the Education Law Center adjust them for regional cost differences.

Teachers are schools’ biggest expense, and salaries vary geographically. A dollar in the Bay Area of California, for example, doesn’t pay for as many teachers as a dollar in rural Alabama.

To show how these adjustments make school funding appear more regressive, the Urban Institute lets readers compare the difference in per-pupil spending with and without adjustments for teacher labor costs.

EdBuild went further, adjusting for a broader basket of regional costs, including housing prices. That can make a dollar in an expensive metropolitan area worth even less than raw dollar spending figures indicate.

Reber also adjusted spending for teacher costs in the appendix of the Brookings’ report. Nonwhite districts spent more per pupil, but their higher teacher salaries left them with about the same purchasing power, she found.

“That changes your way of thinking about where the inequality comes from,” said Reber. “You’re thinking about high labor costs instead of local property tax wealth, which is the story that comes out of the EdBuild report.”

3. Poor children and nonwhite children aren’t interchangeable

Poverty and race overlap, but their school funding stories diverge. Many poor children attend predominantly white, rural schools. Black and Hispanic students are disproportionately poor, but they’re more concentrated in cities, where teacher labor costs are higher.

Adjusting for the high cost of urban teachers can have a bigger effect on the figures for students of color than the figures for poor students. In other words, a district can spend more dollars per pupil but not be able to pay for as many teachers or aides.

That’s a big reason that several reports conclude that poor students are getting more money while Black and Hispanic students are getting less. EdTrust, for example, which released its latest school funding report last month, found that districts serving mostly Black, Hispanic and Native American students got $1,300 fewer state and local dollars per student than white students. But districts serving poor students actually got $200 more a year than nonpoor students.

The school finance economists and advocates I spoke with all said that the funding of poor schools has improved considerably over the decades. But they also agreed that poor children still need more resources to have the same educational opportunities as wealthier children: more counselors, school psychologists, tutors, reading coaches and experienced teachers. Bruce Baker of the University of Miami once estimated that it can cost tens of thousands more per pupil a year to catch poor children’s skills up to the national average in reading and math.

Even Reber, whose research found that poor students receive more money than wealthier students, isn’t satisfied. “Do districts serving children in poverty have what they need? The answer is not universally no, but it’s often no,” she said.

And there’s an even bigger inequity: How much we invest in a child’s education depends enormously on the state where that child is born. New York, the highest-spending state, spends $17,000 more per student than Idaho, according to the Education Law Center’s 2025 report. Regardless of poverty or race, kids in many states get far less.

So whenever someone says poor schools get more or less money, I plan to ask three questions: Which money? Adjusted for what? And compared with whom?

*Update: After publication of this article, Brookings’ Sarah Reber notified The Hechinger Report that she had revised her statement to reflect her updated calculations. It was not always true, over the past two decades, that the highest poverty districts spent more than the lowest poverty districts; from 2012 to 2017, the highest-poverty districts spent about the same as the lowest-poverty districts.

title: As Government Encroaches, Presidents Must ‘Lead the Sector’
summary:
As Government Encroaches, Presidents Must ‘Lead the Sector’
Emma Whitford Mon, 11/09/2026 - 03:00 AM

In their new book, The Postliberal University, Brendan Cantwell and Barrett Taylor explain why university leaders must be explicit in laying out the threats to higher education today.

Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
Higher education governance experts Brendan Cantwell and Barrett Taylor said their new book was tough to write. Over the past two years, they tried to keep up with the churn of higher education news, each headline more outrageous than the last—federal agencies slashed research funding, the Trump administration launched dozens of probes into university admissions practices and state governments got directly involved in curriculum and shared governance, to name a few noteworthy developments.

“There was a temptation to serve as a kind of news aggregator, but that’s not what we wanted to do,” said Taylor, a professor of higher education at the University of North Texas. “We’re professors. It’s our job to understand the broader underlying systems at work here.”

So instead of trying to analyze the news, they sought to “explain how we got to this point, and then offer a robust way to think about what will happen from here,” Taylor said.

The resulting book, The Postliberal University (Harvard Education Press, 2026), provides a framework for readers looking to understand the news they’re reading, said Cantwell, who teaches about higher education and education policy at Michigan State University. The book examines the partisan forces that have shaped higher education governance over the past several decades and offers university leaders concrete ideas about how to preserve the mission of higher ed and steer their institutions—and the sector as a whole—through this period of increasing government meddling.

Inside Higher Ed spoke with Cantwell and Taylor over Zoom about the book, the differences between neoliberal and postliberal governance, and how higher education leaders should meet the moment.

The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Inside Higher Ed: Many higher ed news events over the past year have been called unprecedented, but as you were looking back, are there any precedents that you identified which other people missed?

Taylor: It’s true that things are unprecedented because things are moving really fast and escalating. We did identify, I think, quite a few precedents for ways in which states have systematically expanded their authority over higher education and constrained the capacity of the academic profession—people who work on campuses—to shape decision-making in higher education. That expansion of state authority into areas like curriculum and personnel helps to explain a lot about some of the newsier items coming out of the federal government over the last couple of years … Those state actions also helped to explain how governments—and a slice of the public—became suspicious about the ways higher education had operated, and [why state leaders] began to develop this new way of governing higher education.

Inside Higher Ed: What defines a neoliberal university versus a postliberal one?

Cantwell: We wrote a book in 2019, and we worked very hard to avoid the term “neoliberal,” in part because that term had been used so loosely in our field and others to describe everything we don’t like. Well, we actually embraced it in this book because we saw it as an opportunity to delineate the goals of higher education and the general understanding of how those goals should be pursued. So the neoliberal university—or neoliberal governance—is a higher education that is oriented towards private goods: getting people jobs, generating wealth, contributing to innovation and doing things efficiently. It’s a higher education that was pretty expansive and open and had the idea that more and more people should be involved.

Under these conditions, where the goal was to deliver on mostly economic outcomes, higher education was organized through competition. Competition, accountability and indirect government steering through things like performance funding were used to direct colleges and universities from a distance and orient them towards … private good outcomes. That way of thinking about higher education—while there’s lots of elements to it that are still active today—is really receding, and a new way of thinking about higher education and governing higher education is emerging.

Taylor: We use the concept of a “governance accord” to talk about the goal, as Brendan put it, and then the means of pursuing that goal [through] downstream policy and implementation. The easiest way to think about the shift from neoliberal to postliberal governance is as a move away from that private good goal toward what we call the partisan good. We define the partisan good in two senses. First, it is a broad understanding that higher education should be more subject to political control—that governing coalitions at the state level should have and exercise more authority over public universities. That’s largely a bipartisan project. It looks different in red states, blue states and purple states, but in a variety of states, governments are expanding their control and their authority over higher education in more direct ways than the indirect competition steering that characterizes neoliberalism.

The second sense of the partisan good [looks at specifics]—because there are two major political parties in the U.S. and they’re doing very different things. Republican-controlled states have generally been much more aggressive and intervened much further in matters like curriculum, shared governance, faculty working conditions and teaching and learning than have Democratic or divided governments. So, they’re doing very different things, but they’re all expanding authority over higher education.

If we think about performance-based funding or outcomes-based funding as a steering mechanism, implicit in that is a sense that higher education is not trustworthy to fulfill its objectives—that it needs to be held to account. If those don’t seem to be working, then maybe states take a more direct steering approach to accountability. Particularly, but not exclusively, in red states, I think that starts to happen.

Inside Higher Ed: In the book, you talk about a “neoliberal Trojan horse.” What does that mean, and what are some examples?

Taylor: We use the phrase “neoliberal Trojan horse” to refer to an initiative or an effort that is consistent with the postliberal goal of the partisan good, but that is cloaked or made legible in terms that would be familiar to neoliberal governments. If you are someone who has—as I have—been around higher education for a while, you’re steeped in neoliberal assumptions and ways of operating. When someone says, “We need to do this because it will make higher education more efficient,” or “because it will increase return on investment,” that is hard to contest, because a default assumption for several decades now under neoliberal governance has been that that’s the purpose of higher education … A neoliberal veneer over something that has a postliberal goal within it—that’s where we use the phrase “neoliberal Trojan horse.”

Cantwell: A couple of examples might be laws that have passed in several states that direct universities to conduct reviews and eliminate programs based on enrollment. [Laws] focusing on efficiency and making sure that it’s a good value for money spent on the program—I’m thinking of Iowa and Ohio, for example—are often paired with laws that take a more direct role in reshaping the curriculum through civic centers and changing the general education requirements. So you have this one law that is leading to the closure of programs that the state does not like using a means that seems more palatable, more legitimate. A neoliberal Trojan horse is often accompanied by other kinds of more direct controls; you welcome the horse in, and then the [direct controls] of the state jump out.

Inside Higher Ed: You conducted a survey for the book, which found that a lot of the public skepticism about the sector is centered on whether higher ed shares someone’s values, and not necessarily doubts about cost or efficiency. How does that finding change how universities should be making their case to the public?

Taylor: It’s a pretty succinct way to think about the change from neoliberal to postliberal governance. Under neoliberal governance—because it’s a private good model and the focus is on efficiently delivering those benefits—the most common response to public skepticism or critique has been to say, “We have a really high return on investment. Our graduates earn good wages. We’re doing what we can to make our education affordable.” All of those things demonstrate efficiency and suggest that private returns are, in fact, delivered. But that is very unlikely to assuage the doubts of someone who says, “I think this university does not share my values,” or “I think this part of the university operation does not share my values.”

If you can imagine a state official who expresses skepticism over the existence of a gender studies program, demonstrating that graduates of that program earn high wages is unlikely to persuade that person to keep the program open. That’s not the critique they were leveling. What they were saying is “I don’t think gender studies should be offered at the university.” And so, I think the fact that such a large share of respondents indicated that they didn’t perceive higher education as sharing their values is a pretty clear indicator that continuing to talk about efficient delivery of private benefits is using the rules of the previous governance accord to try and build trust, rather than the rules of the current one.

Cantwell: There are presidents who realize this value gap is a problem. I would point to Ron Daniels at Johns Hopkins as an example, but his response has been to say, “You know what? The public is right and we need to pivot to a more conservative university.” That is one way to respond. Another way to respond might be to say, “Hey, let’s build some internal consensus about what our values are inside the university, with the university as it is, and then work on communicating with community groups, with the general public, with members of the State Legislature about what it is that our values actually are and how we’re living them.” Not so much a defense, but clarifying what it is that the university does and why it does things that way to help bridge some of the gap between what people think the university is and why they think that is out of line with their values.

Inside Higher Ed: You urge presidents to lead higher education and not just their university. What does that look like in practice?

Taylor: Anytime there’s this kind of social disruption, there are going to be opportunities for some folks to take advantage of that and try to improve their own position—the position of their university, the position of their unit. Under neoliberal governance, that was very strongly encouraged. Your goal as a unit leader or a university leader or a system leader was to improve your competitive position relative to other units or universities or systems. We increasingly think the hostility that higher education faces—while individuals and institutions feel it oftentimes very acutely—really is directed at higher education itself as a social institution.

So, if a leader of a university looks at this disruption and says, “Here’s an opportunity for me to improve my university status by taking advantage of some of these new opportunities,” that might help a particular university to climb the rankings, and that might be good for that individual president or unit administrator’s career. But it is not good for higher education at a time when the entire sector is facing these intrusions from state government that make it harder to deliver on the benefits that we are supposed to deliver. And so we’re trying to encourage those folks to lead the sector rather than just their particular unit—to think about higher education itself as being under attack, and what they can do to support higher education rather broadly.

Cantwell: Higher education leaders could help to support the enterprise and help move us into a kind of new place, beyond where we are now, by starting to be quite honest about what they see as the direction of particular state governments and of the federal government.

For example, I see efforts to roll back the desegregation and inclusion initiatives that have taken place in this country since at least the mid-’60s as one of the possible goals of the second definition of the partisan good—where the Republican Party has an idea about the way society should look and who society should serve—and I think that higher education leaders might help to build some credibility if they were willing to lay out the stakes more clearly. This is about a return to a pre–civil rights era version of higher education, and what was that era like? It was smaller. Many fewer people participated in higher education. It was structured by race and gender. It involved many fewer connections with people from around the world, and those connections have led to a dynamic expansion of the science system in the United States and globally. You don’t have to explain it in an alarmist way. You don’t even have to explain it in an explicitly moral or political way, but lay it out as what is happening. Any serious analysis of some federal and state policies lead you to that conclusion.

title: New in AI: UChicago Rethinks Writing, EIU Students Want Faculty Rules
summary:
New in AI: UChicago Rethinks Writing, EIU Students Want Faculty Rules
kathryn.palmer… Mon, 11/09/2026 - 03:00 AM

Inside Higher Ed breaks down some of the latest developments regarding AI and ed tech on campus.

Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
While many universities have announced more artificial intelligence–focused initiatives this fall, one is creating a space designed to help college students develop their own ideas and express them in an authentic voice with—and without—the use of the technology.

Late last month, the University of Chicago launched the Chicago Center for Writing, which is designed to “enrich the teaching and practice of writing” across the university by “advancing writing as an intellectual, creative and collaborative practice,” the university said in a news release.

“The center will provide a throughline for the practice and pedagogy of writing across the University at a time when rapid technological change is raising new questions about how we write, learn and teach,” Abigail Reardon, executive director of the center, said. “Our goal is to extend Chicago’s rich culture of writing by making more space for the practice of writing itself and for thinking together about the often solitary work of drafting and revising.”

Beginning next fall, all first-year students will be required to take an AI-free writing course administered through the center. The center is also developing other writing courses, writing labs and campus partnerships that will allow students and faculty to “experiment with the practices and technologies of writing, both old and new.”

But as faculty all over the country are recognizing, integrating AI into their teaching and research processes can be murky. In fact, the entire higher education landscape is awash with AI-related debates, developments and dustups, which is why Inside Higher Ed is gathering some recent noteworthy happenings in a new monthly roundup.

So far this fall, students and faculty are trying to figure out what appropriate AI use looks like.

AI Backlash: At the same time that faculty are trying to keep original thought at the center of students’ written work, students also want to ensure that faculty aren’t relying too much on AI.

In September, students at Eastern Illinois University started a petition against AI in the classroom. While the university has policies on how students can use AI in their coursework, “we have nothing preventing professors from using AI as a substitute for learning materials,” reads the petition, which had 529 signatures as of Sunday. “This is ultimately problematic as AI is unreliable as a source, and by using it gives the impression that our course material is not important, and takes away value from our education.” By early October, the EIU Student Senate had passed a resolution calling on administrators to regulate faculty AI use.

And just a couple of weeks after that, on Oct. 28 the resignation of Dartmouth College Provost Santiago Schnell showed why having clear guidelines in place may help faculty navigate the murky waters of using AI as a writing tool.

Schnell stepped down about a month after the student newspaper ran several of his articles through an AI detector, which flagged them as partially AI-generated and fueled calls for his firing. A subsequent internal review determined his attempts at disclosing his AI use weren’t in line with the college’s ethics policies, though Schnell’s lawyer has since told The Washington Post that he was not “afforded a meaningful opportunity to present his account” during the review.

Fighting AI With AI? Faculty who are trying to preserve the traditional writing process are increasingly turning to handwritten assignments. But a University of California, Berkeley, graduate student who was tasked with grading such papers noticed that grading was time-consuming and sometimes inconsistent. Earlier this year, Travis Fraser used AI to build Rubrica, a secure platform that grades handwritten exams based on an instructor’s rubric. Although the instructor reviews the results before issuing a final grade, a small study showed that 85 percent of Rubrica’s scores matched human scores.

AI Embrace: A few instances of AI backlash haven’t stopped many other universities from moving forward with investing in AI.

title: Ugly History Doesn’t Mean Faculty Should Reject Civil Discourse Education
summary:
Ugly History Doesn’t Mean Faculty Should Reject Civil Discourse Education
Elizabeth Redden Mon, 11/09/2026 - 03:00 AM

Rather than cede leadership in this area to top-down civics schools or centers, faculty should come up with our own approaches.

Byline(s)
Robert D. Taber
full_text:
Iowa became the latest state to have its flagship campus’s civics center generate embarrassing headlines when 11 faculty resigned from its advisory board—and then again when the choice for center director declined the job, two weeks after his hire was announced. Teaching students how to follow evidence and work with others to solve big problems should not be a controversial proposition. Despite what we see in the news, most faculty just want students to show up to class and engage with the course content.

So why the controversy, to which my home university system is not immune?

Too many universities, public and private, have attempted to present civil discourse as a top-down program, led by boards and presidents, with faculty expected to accept the initiative as a fait accompli. The involvement of Republican lawmakers in the creation of stand-alone civics centers or schools like Iowa’s only exacerbates this problem, fueling accusations of partisan interference in the curriculum. Faculty, aware of those who want to use civil discourse initiatives to replace the existing teaching staff, push back, with some faculty alleging that a “civility industrial complex” has nefarious motives. They rightly point to the ugly ways opponents of civil rights have used appeals to “civility” to shut down discussion and stifle dissent.

But faculty should not reject civil discourse as a concept. Instead, we should propose our own approaches, drawn from our disciplinary expertise and experience in the classroom.

I teach American history, the good and the bad, to a diverse and wide-ranging student body at a regional public university in North Carolina that is also one of the oldest historically Black universities in the U.S. South. My students have robust, evidence-based conversations about difficult topics all the time.

And for the last 11 months, I and other faculty from across North Carolina have helped the University of North Carolina system develop an approach to promoting civil discourse education that is faster, cheaper and more effective than setting up civic centers or top-down programs one by one. Our systemwide task force in civil discourse outlined this approach in our recent report, “Civil Discourse and the University of North Carolina.”

The Context for This Work

Our task force came into the work acutely aware of three dynamics:

The antidemocratic uses of appeals to civility. We grappled with works such as Alex Zamalin’s Against Civility and William Henry Chafe’s Civilities and Civil Rights, both of which are cited in our report.

The debates around UNC Chapel Hill’s School of Civic Life and Leadership, and the ways in which the centers approach is limited to students who opt in, and often, due to the centers’ cost, only students at flagship institutions. If civil discourse is worth teaching, then it is worth bringing to our regional campuses and to students across disciplines in a meaningful way.

That there is stakeholder—and faculty—interest in helping our students sustain dialogue across perceived differences and to address student self-censorship in the classroom. Some of this interest is born from worries about increasing political polarization; quite a bit is from concerns about the impacts of algorithmic social media and pandemic-era disruptions in socialization on our students. Being a student who is hesitant to speak up in 2026, when every classmate—theoretically—has the ability to record your comments and publish them is a very different experience from being a college student in 2001 or 1976. Additionally, we heard from employers that they want graduates to have stronger skills in critical thinking, problem-solving, communication, leadership and teamwork, all attributes that can be built through civil discourse education.

As our task force convened, we also discovered a fair amount of skepticism, including among ourselves. The task force, our colleagues and partners had good-faith discussions about what we mean by civil discourse, its connection with existing disciplines and departments, and if civil discourse is worth doing, how it might be done in a substantive way—more than a student orientation training on “being nice.”

Our Interventions

Our report makes two major interventions that, together, point to an important pathway for better civil discourse education, one that draws on our disciplinary expertise and experience in public university classrooms.

First, instead of providing a two-sentence definition of civil discourse education at the postsecondary level, we frame civil discourse as the overlap of three related concepts. Civil discourse prioritizes strong civility. It is rooted in a culture of collaborative problem-solving. And it respects the inherent dignity of all participants.

Strong civility is good-faith conversation that can contain information that is uncomfortable for one or more participants to hear, but it is done in the pursuit of equitable and inclusive dialogue, with a priority on maintaining underlying relationships for the long haul. It stands in contrast to weak civility, which is politeness for politeness’s sake, and pseudo-civility, which is when people appeal to weak civility to silence attempts at strong civility.

In their Foundations of American Democracy courses, UNC system undergraduates already receive an introduction to one of the most famous distinctions between strong and weak civility. The only 20th-century document required by the system’s course objectives is Martin Luther King Jr.’s “Letter From Birmingham Jail.” Responding to clergy upset at the tumult they think was caused by civil rights protesters, King differentiates between a “negative peace which is the absence of tension” and a “positive peace which is the presence of justice.”

Our focus on fostering a culture of problem-solving draws from a long literature on the role of the public university in the formation of citizens, concerns about the gamification or performance of civility to check a box, and an awareness that only presenting students with problems and then throwing up our hands can be dispiriting. If citizenship involves tackling common challenges, then the work we are doing as faculty to expand students’ capacity for citizenship should take that into account. This framework also helps expand “civil discourse” to include “easy conversations,” interdisciplinary projects, service learning and practicums, not just structured debates, though those also have their place and can help with problem-solving.

Respecting the inherent dignity of participants—including by not questioning their right to be students on campus—recognizes that students are all members of the same university community and that even the words we use to talk about civil discourse can cause mistrust. Learning and practicing language rooted in dignity, however, helps build trust and end high conflict.

Knowing what civil discourse education is, however, does not tell us where in the university it can or should happen. This is where so many institutions go wrong.

The second major intervention is that while good civil discourse teaching can occur within many different academic disciplines, universities wanting a fast, effective and sustainable increase in civil discourse training for their students should reinvest in pre-existing departments in the humanities, arts and related social sciences. Universities could even hire more tenure-track faculty in history, classics, English literature, philosophy, government and, yes, world languages. Encourage students to take electives beyond the core curriculum.

If the point of a civil discourse push is to provide education for a free people, then that education should happen in the context of the disciplines that introduce students to the breadth and depth of the human experience.

How the Report Has Been Received

We released our initial report in June. Two months later, UNC System President Peter Hans and Board of Governors Chair Kellie Hunt Blue cited it by name in their official response to Secretary of Education Linda McMahon’s “National Call to Action to University Presidents and Governing Boards.”

The UNC system has also awarded more than $500,000 in grants to faculty to design new courses or redesign existing ones related to the teaching of civil discourse through its Common Ground Collaborative. While this is a sizable investment, it is one that can be done in-house, without special legislative appropriations. The system has now provided 119 grants to 126 faculty at all 17 UNC system campuses; this has been so successful that the system is committing another round of funding for the coming academic year. Compare that, however, to the $59 million being used to create civics institutes on five campuses in Ohio.

Beyond the grants, the Common Ground Collaborative’s convening this past May at UNC Charlotte drew together 100 faculty to share best practices, for the cost of a couple of meals and some support for in-state travel.

Beyond North Carolina

Faculty wanting to engage in teaching civil discourse will not lack ideas about useful approaches. This past summer, Campus Compact, the American Association of Colleges and Universities, More Perfect and the University of Virginia’s Karsh Institute of Democracy launched the Higher Education Democracy Exchange, which offers teaching, programming and research resources. The UNC report contains links to many more.

title: How to navigate AI adoption — with faculty and student input
summary: Artificial intelligence is transforming the mission of public education and “can’t just be implemented one way from the top,” one instructor said.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Colleges and universities nationwide have faced waves of student protests pushing back on institutional policies that embrace the use of artificial intelligence tools on campus.

That includes students and faculty at Columbia University who in May railed against the use of AI to announce graduates' names during commencement ceremonies, and students and employees at Emory University who in April called on administrators to remove AI-powered surveillance cameras from campus.

Universities have used AI tools to assist with a host of administrative functions, such as scheduling courses and nudging students to register for classes. In addition, many college officials are pushing to embed instruction on AI into curricula as businesses increasingly use generative AI platforms like OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini.

The embrace of AI has caused tension among students and faculty wary about its environmental, ethical, pedagogical, social and academic integrity impacts, said Victor Lee, faculty lead at the Stanford Accelerator for Learning's initiative to support educators in navigating the AI era.

Holding intentional conversations with students and faculty about AI use on campus can help ease concerns, said Lee.

Faculty members aren’t necessarily opposed to the technology, experts say, but training on the tools is spotty and they would like to be part of conversations about how their institutions use AI.

Robert Ovetz, a San José State University professor, is among the faculty members who have vocally opposed universities integrating AI into curricula with little to no input from faculty or their unions.

“This is the transformation of the very mission of public education, and it can’t just be implemented one way from the top,” said Ovetz, who is co-author of the forthcoming book “Organizing Against AI in Higher Education.”

Institutional support for AI

SJSU formally launched an initiative called AI Everywhere in fall 2025 with the aim of ethically and responsibly integrating the technology throughout campus. The initiative is part of an effort to prepare students for the future workforce, said Sandra Hirsh, the university's special assistant to the provost for AI initiatives.

It’s also part of a larger push by the California State University system, which signed contracts with several AI-focused tech companies in 2025, including a nearly $17 million deal with Open AI to provide ChatGPT Edu to more than 460,000 students and 63,000 faculty and staff throughout its 22 campuses. CSU renewed its contract with OpenAI this year to the tune of $13 million annually for three years.

By the start of the 2027-28 academic year, SJSU expects to have 28 AI-related programs and 101 courses, Hirsh said. That would represent a 75% and 36% increase, respectively, since fall 2025.

The university also launched a host of new AI events and initiatives, including faculty training on one of tech company Nvidia’s platforms. In the same vein, it worked with the city of San Jose to open the AI Center for Civic and Social Good, a space at a joint public and university academic library where community residents, students and workers can use AI education tools, Hirsh said.

"This is the transformation of the very mission of public education, and it can’t just be implemented one way from the top."

Robert Ovetz

Professor at San José State University

While the scale of SJSU's AI efforts are significant, it's hardly the only institution to embrace the technology. Almost every institution is using or plans to use AI in some capacity, said Hironao Okahana, formerly managing researcher and chief of planning and impact at the American Council on Education.

In many places, that has translated into new courses. Over one-third of surveyed faculty members, 37%, said their institution had created new AI-focused classes, according to a report released in January by the American Association of Colleges and Universities and Elon University, which polled over 1,000 instructors in fall 2025.

And as of last July, a quarter of senior higher ed leaders reported adopting generative AI technologies at their institutions for student support, with another 22% planning to do so within the next six months, according to an ACE fall 2025 survey. Another 43% said they planned to adopt AI technologies within the next one to two years.

Broad concerns with AI

Many students, meanwhile, have issues with the ways large language models use data without their knowledge and consent, and how these systems reproduce and amplify existing forms of discrimination in society, among a host of other concerns, said Lindsay Weinberg, a professor and director of Purdue University’s Tech Justice Lab.

And some students are apprehensive about their universities forging partnerships with companies that use AI for military purposes, Weinberg said.

In April, SJSU students protested their university’s ties to companies includingNvidia, OpenAI, and Google for that reason, Spartan Media Group reported.

Many faculty share the students' concerns. And both faculty and students express misgivings about the environmental consequences from AI and how data centers cause noise pollution and negatively impact local water and electrical systems, said Weinberg.

Students are also hearing widespread reports about how AI will automate entry-level jobs, shrinking their job opportunities, Ovetz added.

Unease regarding education quality

Faculty have broad worries on AI’s impact on higher education, said C. Edward Watson, vice president for digital innovation at AAC&U and co-author of the association’s faculty survey report.

Nearly 52% of staff and faculty at CSU institutions indicated they were skeptical of the benefits of AI in higher education, with about 85% indicating they were concerned about the ethical use of the technology, according to 2025 system survey data.

A nationwide survey from AAC&U also highlighted additional sweeping concerns from faculty. About three-quarters of faculty said cheating spiked on their campuses when generative AI tools became widespread and that they believed the technology would impact degree integrity.

Meanwhile, nearly all faculty members, 95%, expressed concern about students becoming overreliant on AI tools, and large majorities indicated the technology would diminish students’ critical thinking skills and attention spans, according to the report.

Overall, Ovetz said, many educators say that by using AI, students are cheating themselves out of the reasons they are attending college — to learn and expand their understanding, consciousness and awareness.

For some students, their opposition to AI is part of broader resistance to technology and social media shifting from being optional to seemingly mandatory in today’s society — including on campuses, said Lucy Jackson, a sophomore at Binghamton University, in New York.

Jackson was an early member of the Luddite Club, a New York City-based anti-tech youth group that has turned into a global movement with roughly 40 campus and regional chapters over the past five years.

When students enroll at a university, they are expecting to receive an education, not a requirement that they have to interact with certain technologies, said Jackson.

But some students are using AI tools to help with their homework or exams, giving them an unfair advantage, and getting a “way out of education” — allowing them to earn a degree “without having to do much,” Jackson said.

“That creates a culture that isn’t necessarily something that everybody wants to live in or that everyone wants to follow,” said Jackson. “That’s where a lot of the pushback comes from.”

Support for AI literacy

Despite the concerns, faculty aren’t broadly rejecting AI tools, Ovetz said. Many view generative AI as an interesting tool to incorporate into their teaching, for example by using chatbots to help students engage with course material, said Ovetz.

At CSU, 61% of faculty and staff said they regularly use AI-powered tools or applications when teaching, researching or performing their work, and 64% say it positively affects those tasks, according to the survey of CSU campuses.

Higher ed leaders have been grappling with how to integrate AI literacy into the curriculum, who should be teaching courses on how to use AI, what type of professional development should be required for instructors and what type of tools they should provide to faculty and students, Watson said.

While colleges and universities are good at adding new courses to meet student needs,they are not good at doing it fast, said Watson. It usually takes a few semesters of discussions with faculty and employers to determine what students need to know, he said.

That was reflected in the AAC&U survey, with 68% of faculty reporting their institutions had not prepared educators to use generative AI “for effective teaching and mentoring.” Less than half reported their institutions had written guidelines for AI use, and just 13% had adopted AI literacy as “a general learning outcome.”

That’s despite a widespread belief among faculty members that it’s important to teach students about issues related to AI during class, the AAC&U survey found. Large majorities stated it was important to teach students about inaccurate statements produced by GenAI tools, how the tools are used to produce misinformation and deep fakes, and how they erode copyright and authorship, according to the survey.

It has been largely left to individual professors to design or restructure their courses with AI, said Lee. The vast majority of faculty, 87%, said they have created their own policies on students’ use of generative AI for assessments, projects and tests, the survey found.

That’s not surprising, however, as decisions about what faculty teach are not usually made top-down, Lee said.

“The law and philosophy of academic freedom and trusting the learning expertise of the faculty leaves a little bit more of a hands-off orientation,” Lee said.

A collaborative process?

When administrators form partnerships with tech companies and push technologies without discussing those initiatives with unions or faculty members on their campuses, they often draw the ire of the students and employees most impacted by those decisions, said Weinberg.

Last year, the California Faculty Association filed an unfair labor practice charge against CSU, alleging the university system failed to notify the union when it launched an AI initiative in 2025 and refused to meet to discuss faculty rights and the impacts that it would have. CFA represents some 29,000 professors, lecturers and other workers at CSU.

The union complaint underscored the need for administrators to slow down on AI adoption so those initiatives can go through the shared governance process and be bargained over with academic unions, said Ovetz, who has been involved in the bargaining efforts.

CFA in February introduced an article in their negotiations with the university to protect faculty from being required to use the tools and provide them with intellectual property protections. Those negotiations have been ongoing for a year and a half, said Ovetz, but no agreement or contract has yet been reached.

“We are planning to vote to strike in the coming months, including over AI,” Ovetz said.

Those protections are important, as workloads increase for faculty who have to learn how to use AI tools as well as constantly check students' work to see if it was written using the technology, said Ovetz.

Many institutions that have succeeded in integrating AI for teaching or administrative purposes have established universitywide committees that discuss new pieces of technology and goals for using them, said Okahana. Those committees should include various campus stakeholder and constituent groups to help get people on board with new technologies, he said.

SJSU, for example, formed a 15-member AI advisory committee in 2024 composed of various university stakeholders, including faculty, students and staff, to advise administrators on how to ethically integrate AI tools throughout campus.

More than half of faculty reported their institutions had implemented a task force or group to oversee and manage implementation of AI tools across their campus, according to the AAC&U survey.

“Stakeholder engagement is really important and not just a tool to plug in,” said Okahana. “It is challenging us to think about how we do the teaching, how we run the university.”

Ovetz, however, said an advisory committee “is just that: advisory.”

An investigation into a private religious school accused of mishandling allegations of sexual, physical, psychological, spiritual and financial abuse has recommended it be barred from enrolling new students.

Former students and teachers of western Sydney’s Redeemer Baptist school told a New South Wales parliamentary inquiry about a string of disturbing allegations.

They included students being made to share beds with teachers and its principal once wandering naked through a common area.

In a report tabled in state parliament on Tuesday, a committee found the school – run by the Redeemer Baptist Church – breached basic child safeguarding standards.

Sexual assault allegations were not handled appropriately and the school put children at significant risk of harm, the committee found.

It also found staff at the school lacked essential workplace rights and failed to satisfy basic standards of good governance.

The committee recommended the school be prevented from enrolling new students while it was under investigation by the NSW Education Standards Authority.

It also recommended the allegations raised in the inquiry be investigated by NSW police and the office of the children’s guardian.

The committee chair and Greens MP, Abigail Boyd, noted the school was subjected to parliamentary scrutiny in 2006, but no procedures had been put in place to monitor what was clearly a “high-risk situation”.

She said it was thanks to the bravery of those who had spoken out that the committee had enough evidence to make its strong findings and recommendations.

The school received about $6m a year in government funding, Boyd said, and had enough cash to launch legal challenges against those who raised their voices against the religious group.

“They also have deep political ties with both state and federal politicians,” she told parliament.

People who had escaped the school appeared to be absolutely terrified of its leaders, Boyd said.

“When you know that leaving means leaving with no financial assets, and when you have finally managed to escape, it’s no wonder that you would be terrified of your abuser,” she said in parliament.

The committee lashed a lack of regulatory oversight, including from the education authority, suggesting a number of alarming matters needed proper investigation.

They included allegations of persistent Centrelink fraud and dodgy tax practices.

“It is, at the very least, troubling that an asset-rich, seemingly prosperous school operates by withholding wages from its workforce, who claim benefits, while the school receives millions of dollars in public funding,” the report said.

A Redeemer Baptist school spokesperson previously said the school had fully cooperated with the relevant regulators.

“Redeemer Baptist School takes its child safety obligations extremely seriously and has an unblemished record of compliance with state and federal regulators for 45 years,” they said.

The school did not immediately respond to a request for comment following the report’s release.
