title: Plagiarism is a kind of theft, but it is also a question of honour
summary: The essay has been virtually obliterated as a form of assessment by the promiscuous use students make of AI. These students are plagiarists.
full_text:
Any concept that has a history, philosopher Michel Foucault tells us, cannot have a fixed definition.

Plagiarism is a concept with a history, as the subtitle of Roger Kreuz’s Strikingly Similar: Plagiarism and Appropriation from Chaucer to Chatbots reminds us. But it might be close to perennial.

Review: Strikingly Similar: Plagiarism and Appropriation from Chaucer to Chatbots – Roger Kreuz (Cambridge University Press)

As a term describing literary, artistic or intellectual theft, “plagiarism” is derived from one of the epigrams of the ancient Roman poet Martial:

Quintianus, I commend you my little books – that is, however, if I can call them mine when your poet friend recites them. If they complain of harsh enslavement, come forward to claim their freedom and give bail as required. And when he calls himself their owner, say they are mine, discharged from my hand. If you shout this three or four times, you will make the kidnapper ashamed of himself.

The Latin word for “kidnapper” Martial uses is plagiario, which gives us the English term “plagiarism”. Other Roman writers, like Cicero, already familiar with the phenomenon of literary theft, used different terms like furtum (a trick) and surripio (taking something secretly), which cover a range of connotations.

The Statute of Anne

Much ink has been spilled over the question of whether the ways we understand plagiarism are continuous with the classical notions that gave us the term, or whether there has been a rupture (or several).

The most often cited candidate is the Statute of Anne (1710), the first effort by a government anywhere to codify copyright and make it enforceable under the law.

Copyright, the argument goes, emanates from the rumbustious commercial culture of Restoration England. It encourages us to think about literary texts as a form of capital, valuable for their ability to generate income for their creators and their creators’ descendants.

Medieval and early modern attitudes towards appropriation differed from later ones. Witness the massive profusion of Aristotle’s ideas throughout medieval philosophy, for instance, or Shakespeare’s avid lifting of plots from historians Holinshed and Plutarch.

But, equally, who would deny the enormous ingenuity that transformed Aristotelianism into the Summa Theologica of Thomas Aquinas, or the chronicles of Holinshed into King Lear?

There is an important slippage here, the one telegraphed in Kreuz’s subtitle: from plagiarism to appropriation. Renaissance philosopher Francis Bacon railed against the “idols of the theatre”, his name for dogmas derived from ancient philosophy, assented to only for their antiquity. But Bacon was not accusing anyone of passing off Aristotle’s texts as their own.

Inspiration, allusion, influence, all the textual chains that make up a tradition or a culture: these are complex. They take time and patience to disentangle. Yet plagiarism, as literary critic Christopher Ricks is at pains to remind us, is simple: it is an act of dishonesty. And it has been deprecated as such at every stage of literate culture.

The Statute of Anne did not invent a new understanding of plagiarism grounded in copyright, though it was responding to the new salience of literary theft, as the world of print made the practice easier and, seemingly, more widespread. The great threat to authors’ livelihoods at this time was the pirated edition, rather than theft in the sense of fraudulent attribution (although this took place as well).

Far from representing a rupture with the classical tradition, copyright accentuates a dimension of plagiarism present from the start. It adds a literal theft to the moral injury that Martial’s “kidnapping” characterises as a metaphorical theft.

Ricks underscores another facet of Martial’s tenacious metaphor. The plagiarist does not deprive the originator of the work itself, in the way a thief deprives its owner of the stolen object. In Ricks’ words, the plagiarist “hopes to gain honour from a dishonourable practice”.

For Ricks, this dual aspect of plagiarism is apt to lead us astray. To the extent that we rely on judicial determinations and judicial remedies, we tend to neglect the original sense of moral injury.

The problem of intention

Such is the outline of a historical account of plagiarism. What do we learn from it?

We learn that plagiarism is a simple concept with an unusual degree of historical consistency, but that its connections with neighbouring concepts, such as influence and copyright, can be complex.

We learn that a legalistic or procedural approach to the problem of plagiarism leaves an important dimension of it unaddressed.

A more fine-grained account would also reveal that authors tend to be perpetually in crisis over plagiarism’s perceived prevalence.

For Kreuz, however, plagiarism is an example of what he and his fellow social scientists would call a “fuzzy concept”. He cites a lack of consensus around whether insufficient attribution amounts to the same thing as plagiarism (yes, if the intent was to deceive) and how much copying counts as plagiarism (conceivably any amount, again depending on the intention).

Intention, famously, is hard to establish. As Ricks reminds us, however, this doesn’t make the concept of plagiarism itself unclear.

Questions of allusion and influence, and the point at which knowledge leaves the preserve of its discoverer and joins what Karl Marx called the “general intellect”, are nigh on impossible to legislate in advance. The point was made by philosopher G.W.F Hegel two centuries ago, when he argued that, because such questions “cannot be precisely determined” in strictly legal terms, plagiarism ought to be a “matter of honour, and honour should deter people from committing it”.

How, then, does Kreuz propose to advance our understanding beyond this durable-seeming consensus? He has amassed a database of some 4,600 incidents of plagiarism drawn principally from “journalistic accounts”.

That database has been well used: the substance of the book is a seemingly interminable series of vignettes, drawn from a variety of national contexts (but mostly American), professions and periods. These include, for instance, the infamous 1976 ruling in a music publisher’s case against George Harrison over his song My Sweet Lord, which was found to be an “unconscious plagiarism” of the Chiffons’ 1963 hit He’s So Fine.

Another example is Joe Biden reproducing certain phrases and arguments from a speech by British Labour Party leader Neil Kinnock during the Democratic presidential primaries in 1987. The revelation derailed Biden’s campaign.

But it is unclear what these vignettes are supposed to teach us about the nature of plagiarism, the traits of plagiarists, the nature of originality, and the place of influence. None of the important issues are adjudicated on, or even expanded upon. Instead, they are merely gestured at, before we move swiftly on to another anecdote.

Dishonourable times

The slippage between “plagiarism” and “appropriation” in Kreuz’s preface is constant and neither term is defined. Is the former a subset of the latter? It takes until page 192 for us to learn that plagiarism is a “fuzzy concept”, leaving us to wonder what rules governed inclusion in the database underlying the project.

The book’s marketing and subtitle suggest it tells us something urgent about plagiarism and appropriation in the age of AI. This is false. Its final sentence is another equivocation – namely, that those water-muddying cultural norms might be shifting again in the present.

How? Should they? Kreuz doesn’t say.

Those of us working in the universities have seen, since 2022, the venerable essay virtually obliterated as a form of assessment by the promiscuous use students make of AI. AI cheating is a form of plagiarism: these students have tried (usually successfully) to deceive their teachers that they are the authors of computer-generated prose.

The legalistic, procedural response seems futile. AI detection software is widely judged unreliable. Academic dishonesty procedures are producing insuperable amounts of bureaucratic work, beyond even what even the distended administration of the modern university can absorb.

All that remains is the moral dimension. It would probably do little good to insist to anyone who passes off AI-generated work as their own that they are dishonouring themselves. But that is because we live in a society determined to exterminate every measure of value apart from self-interest. Hegel’s “honour” is at best a quaint vestige of a vanished world.

If we really value intellectual originality, artistic creativity and human excellence, we have to do more than develop better detection tools and oppose AI companies’ pilfering of art, literature, and thought. We have to try to build a society that fosters these values for everyone, not one that tries to commercialise them at best and extirpate them at worst.

Yes, there is often a legal dimension to plagiarism, but there is an irreducible moral dimension as well, and the whole tendency of our society is toward the procedural and legalistic, to the detriment of every other consideration.

Hegel was right: plagiarism has to be a matter of honour. But we live in dishonourable times.

title: ‘I’d always disliked politics’ | An excerpt from Sonia Gandhi’s ‘Belonging: A Journey of Love’
summary: In her memoir, the senior Congress party leader revisits the years of hesitation and personal conflict before duty finally prevailed
full_text:
With Rajiv gone, everything around me echoed and re-echoed my loss. While I found some solace in the tasks centred on his memory, I was confronted with my fragility whenever the need arose to make public appearances. They couldn’t be avoided: there was the work of various memorial trusts that I headed, which had to continue — international conferences and lectures. At such functions I was required to welcome the guests with a speech. I would have to wrestle with my agitation in the preceding days and the fear that tears would overwhelm me suddenly while I was addressing the audience. That would happen also when visitors condoled with me. I remember when His Holiness the Dalai Lama came and asked me in his usual matter-of-fact manner, “Do you feel vengeful towards those who killed Rajiv?” I replied, “No, I don’t,” and burst into sobs.

That vulnerability remained with me for a long time, but slowly, slowly, the days began to feel less empty and endless. Sleep returned. Rajiv became a presence within me rather than a piercing absence in my life, though the anguish returned in force every time we — Rahul and Priyanka as well as I — shared something important, a rite of passage in which he would have been a vital participant — like their graduations, his daughter’s wedding, later the birth of his grandchildren.

Priyanka graduated with a degree in psychology in 1993 from Jesus and Mary College. Rahul graduated with a master of philosophy (M.Phil) degree from Trinity College in 1995. Priyanka and I decided to attend his convocation, and my mother and younger sister joined us with two of my nieces. Rahul could barely contain his happiness when we turned up; beaming from ear to ear, he embraced all six of us.

To be walking again the narrow streets of Cambridge, still thriving and thrumming with students, passing by old haunts — the Varsity restaurant, my old language school, Rajiv’s lodgings on Kimberley Road and mine on Tenison Road — brought back memories of when he and I first met, of our blissful time together. During the moving graduation ceremony in the Senate House, as Rahul received his degree, I struggled to suppress my tears. Rahul and Priyanka were similarly overcome. How they missed their father at that special moment, how proud Rajiv would have felt of his son.

* * *

Time flowed on. As I gradually emerged from seclusion and became a little more active, once in a while Rajiv’s former colleagues would visit — some for a courtesy call, or to invite me to a family function, others with pleas that I take an active interest in party affairs. To the latter I would listen quietly but not heed their request.

The 1996 election results were disappointing for the Congress Party. It had not been able to form a government on its own. It was plagued by splits and factional disputes. In 1995 I had been asked to support one particular group, in which the main actors were Arjun Singh, N.D. Tiwari, and Mohsina Kidwai, who’d been party members for decades and had held important positions and ministries. I had refused. They broke away and formed another party, followed the next year by senior Tamil leaders G.K. Moopanar and P. Chidambaram, and a younger Congress member, Madhavrao Scindia, who’d joined in 1980. All of them set up separate parties. In 1997 Mamata Banerjee left, due to differences with the state leadership, and formed her own party, the Trinamool Congress. I had become a primary member in 1997 when I was invited by the Congress President Sitaram Kesri to the party’s 80th Plenary Session in Calcutta, but as the party’s situation seemed to be worsening, the pressure on me was increasing to take over its leadership.

I began to feel agitated, brooding on what was going on in the Congress Party, worrying about its fate. Articles in the media were painting a sorry picture of its future. Each time I walked past Rajiv’s picture and my mother-in-law’s, a mixture of pain and guilt would seize me; at times I’d even deliberately avoid looking at them. The India of my belonging had come to me through my husband and my mother-in-law. The very forces they had fought against for decades to protect India’s pluralistic ethos were now bent upon a path that would do untold damage. How could I sit comfortably at home and let their work and their sacrifices go in vain?

I felt tormented. I’d wake up in the middle of the night wondering what I should do, asking myself which way I should go. Had I not fought at every step against a life in politics? Had it not cruelly taken away from me first my mother-in-law, then the love of my life, my children’s father? Why, why was I feeling that strong urge to respond to the demand being made of me? I’d always disliked politics, even during all the years when Rajiv was in public life. But now I was beginning to understand what had compelled him, what I had then so strongly resisted: the pull of duty towards his mother, his country. That pull was now getting hold of me. It scared me, I tried to fight it, but it kept coming back to haunt me.

I was caught in a war with myself: part of me recoiled at the world of politics, of the ambition and greed, hypocrisy and treachery that goes inescapably with the game of power everywhere. But I couldn’t repudiate the inner compulsions that had been drilled into me from my childhood — diligence in assigned tasks, respect towards elders, obedience to parents, fidelity to family norms. They kept gnawing at me. Where my duty lay was clear to me; what that implied was the terrifying part.

I’d seen that world. I had experienced it through Rajiv: in its peaks of high endeavour and achievement, as well as in all its ugliness and venality. How could I even think of getting into it? And to lead the party in an impending electoral battle? Where was my experience, where was my ability or understanding of the task — a task that had often frustrated even the tallest leaders of the past? I was after all the outsider. I had been reminded of that status again and again. Yes, I was Indira Gandhi’s daughter-in-law, Rajiv Gandhi’s widow — but how dare I even think of stepping into a party position they had occupied, I asked myself.

I had no right — except for the fact that I carried the family name: a name that had a wide appeal across the country because it signified devoted service and allegiance to the all inclusive ethos of India, above and beyond categories of religion, caste, language, or region. It was for that reason that so many Congress men and women were pleading with me to come forward to head the party; otherwise, it would break up and scatter — as it was now doing. Soon there would be nothing left to hold back the relentless advance of the communal forces, they urged. And that was for me the most compelling argument.

The struggle went on, through nights of broken sleep and anxious days. I felt tortured, alone — longing for something, an anchor to hold on to, someone, something to guide me and help me out of my fears and doubts. Was it a subconscious search that would lead me to where I already knew in my heart I had to go?

I’ve never been religious in all my adult life, though I respect all faiths, but it was during this period that I felt the urge to go back to the Bhagavad Gita. I had read it when I was much younger. The ancient book and the great story of which it was a part were everywhere, permeating the life and thought of millions. I was aware of its profound effect on the heroes of the independence movement. I’d witnessed its representations in theatre, in festivals and other forms. I’d heard its couplets recited again and again by political personalities to make a point or to enlighten.

I knew of the Lal Bahadur Shastri Sanskrit Vidyapeeth. Careful not to disclose the reason for my request, I asked my office to enquire if I could take some classes at home. The name of Professor Vachaspati Upadhyaya — “Shastriji” as we called him, a gentle, unassuming, and erudite scholar who was also known to our family — came up. He kindly agreed to explain the deeper philosophical meaning of the Gita to me in his spare time.

Starting in January 1997, I sat with him periodically over a volume chosen from Rajiv’s bookshelves, a Sanskrit edition with Hindi and English translations below each couplet. Shastriji would recite a verse or two in Sanskrit, I’d read out the Hindi translation, and he’d explain the meaning. We started slowly, but I see from my office appointment diary that in December 1997 we had many sessions. Our readings continued at a pace until our last one, on January 5, 1998.

Rahul and Priyanka were aware of my restlessness and feared I might allow myself to get drawn into politics. Just as I had fought with Rajiv, my two children now argued fiercely with me. They had been through the ordeals of losing their grandmother and their father; there were only the three of us now left of our family; they didn’t want to lose me, too, they said emphatically. They extracted a promise from me before leaving for their New Year vacation: “Happy New Year, Mama. Don’t you do anything crazy while we’re away. You’ve promised us, remember.”

I was on my own now with my churning thoughts. The readings were drawing to a close. Krishna has expounded the message of the Gita: Perform your dharma without regard for the fruit of your action. Arjuna, the Pandava prince, declares that his illusion is now dispelled; he is restored to himself, firm and free from all doubts, and ready to play his part in the battle.

Something awoke in me: I was sure. I had the answer to my own doubts and questions. I had to step out and go where my duty called. And I did.

title: Canada cuts, NZ grows as Australia and US rethink international education
summary:
At AIEC 2026, leaders said policy uncertainty, public trust and student outcomes are redrawing the competition for global talent.

The post Canada cuts, NZ grows as Australia and US rethink international education appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
International education’s most established destinations are no longer following the same script.

Canada is reducing volume while prioritising research talent, New Zealand is pursuing growth within quality safeguards, Australia is seeking greater certainty after a period of policy tightening, and US institutions are being urged to reassess their place in a more multipolar world.

Those divergent paths emerged at AIEC’s Global Dialogue, chaired by Jazreel Goh of the British Council, where leaders repeatedly returned to the limits of a recruitment-led model.

Canada’s reset has been among the most visible. Larissa Bezo, president and CEO of the Canadian Bureau for International Education (CBIE), said a cap on study permits, higher financial requirements and changes to post-study work pathways had pushed international student numbers down to just under 700,000 at the end of 2025, from more than one million at the end of 2023.

“Canada is moving from a conversation about growth to a conversation about sustainability, quality and longer-term impact,” Bezo said.

Canada has also moved to attract more master’s and doctoral students, issuing 6,455 new graduate study permits in the second quarter of 2026, more than double the 3,085 issued during the same period a year earlier.

Graduate students are now exempt from the provincial or territorial attestation letter requirement, while other applicants face higher financial thresholds.

Bezo said institutions had struggled to reach their allocations not simply because of the cap, but because of affordability concerns, changed immigration pathways and a succession of policy signals that had unsettled applicants.

She recalled meeting prospective students in Vietnam after the cap was announced and being asked: “Why did you close the borders?”

That perception matters, she said, even when formal routes remain open, and Canada is now trying to rebuild predictability by being clearer about what students can expect during and after study.

Australia is confronting a related, but distinct, challenge. Phil Honeywood, chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia (IEAA), argued that years of commercial dependence on overseas fees had created a tension between international education’s revenue role and its wider public purpose.

“We’ve got this conundrum of profit motive versus the public good,” Honeywood said, contrasting a recruitment-led approach with the promises of global citizenship, soft power and opportunity for students.

“It’s all about inculcating global citizenship virtues,” he said, describing the approach he heard from European peers.

In October, the Australian government opened a consultation on possible changes to the Genuine Student requirement and financial-capacity rules after assistant minister for international education Julian Hill acknowledged that high refusal rates were deterring students in key markets, particularly South Asia.

The proposals would strengthen financial verification and, under some models, require relevant study funds to be held in Australian bank accounts.

The consultation follows recent restrictions on student dependants, course transfers and some onshore pathways, which sector leaders have warned could compound the impression that Australia has become harder to access.

For Honeywood, the question is whether Australia can show that its international education offer extends beyond migration settings and fee income.

Internationalisation is not just about teaching and learning. It’s also about research collaboration

John Hudzik, Michigan State University

Professor John Hudzik of Michigan State University said American institutions could no longer assume they occupied a default position in global higher education, describing a transition from a bipolar to a multipolar world in which the US must work with other countries as equals. “Business as usual is over,” Hudzik said.

“We count outputs, not outcomes,” Hudzik said, arguing that universities had not sufficiently explained to the public why international students, global research and cross-border partnerships matter.

A Department of Homeland Security proposal would charge universities USD$70,000 for an initial Optional Practical Training recommendation and USD$30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including a STEM extension.

The fees are not in force, but advisers have warned that they could weaken the financial case for loan-funded students, particularly from India, as some applicants add alternative destinations rather than abandon US plans altogether.

New Zealand, meanwhile, is presenting itself as a growth market while stressing that its social licence cannot be taken for granted.

David Downs, chief executive of Education New Zealand Manapou ki te Ao, said the agency had redefined its purpose as “grow New Zealand through international education”, with sustainability, quality and student experience built into that ambition.

“You don’t take your sort of current settings for granted. They can change quite quickly,” Downs said.

New Zealand is on track for about 99,000 international enrolments in 2026, still below its 2019 peak, while export earnings have moved beyond pre-pandemic levels.

Recent national survey data provides a strong foundation for growth, with 90% of international students rating their overall experience positively and 47% describing it as excellent.

But the same survey showed the fragility of that proposition: only 55% rated work experience positively and just 33% said it was easy to find part-time work alongside their studies.

“At the end of it are human beings who are making really serious decisions for their lives,” Downs said.

The panel’s discussion comes as students become less tied to a small group of familiar Anglophone destinations.

Indian advisers say applicants are increasingly taking a portfolio approach, shortlisting three or four countries and comparing cost, visa certainty, employment prospects and return on investment before committing.

Germany, France, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Malaysia, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and the UAE are among the destinations gaining greater attention as the US, Canada, Australia and the UK reassess migration and post-study settings.

At The PIE Live India earlier this year, representatives from France, Germany, Ireland, Malaysia and Japan similarly argued that sustainable growth depended on academic partnerships, graduate outcomes and government-to-government engagement, rather than recruitment volume alone.

That is also changing the institutional task.

Bezo urged universities not to undervalue the staff expertise and relationships needed to sustain international engagement, while Downs cautioned against “scattergunning” across markets and programs without a clear long-term strategy.

Honeywood said universities must also break down faculty silos if internationalisation is to become a genuine institution-wide project rather than a function of recruitment teams.

For Hudzik, mobility cannot remain the sole measure of internationalisation as transnational delivery and research partnerships evolve.

“Internationalisation is not just about teaching and learning,” he said. “It’s also about research collaboration.”

title: UK business schools’ finances strained amid fall in international enrolments
summary:
Almost 70% of UK business schools are reporting a drop in international enrolments, as government policies add pressure to already-strained finances.

The post UK business schools’ finances strained amid fall in international enrolments appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Results from the 2026 Chartered Association of Business Schools Annual Membership Survey show that 69% of responding schools recorded lower international enrolments this academic year, almost double the 35% reported in last year’s survey.

This fall is deemed a serious concern by responding business schools, with almost all reporting some degree of reliance on international student fees to ensure their financial viability.

Postgraduate recruitment has taken the biggest hit, with two-thirds of schools reporting that they were below their recruitment target and 60% recording significantly lower international enrolments.

While the decline was less pronounced at undergraduate level, three in five schools still reported a similar trend.

Government policy towards international students was cited as driving the decline in enrolments, with Stewart Robinson, chair of the Chartered ABS and dean of Newcastle University Business School, saying “the reality” of the policies had “finally hit” and that business schools are “bearing the brunt.”

“The government has rightly asked more of universities, from working more closely with business to playing a key role in driving the government’s own £40bn international education export target. But universities and business schools cannot deliver what is asked of them without the government removing some of the barriers it has placed in their way,” he added.

Universities and business schools cannot deliver what is asked of them without the government removing some of the barriers it has placed in their way

Stewart Robinson, Chartered ABS

The planned reduction in the length of the graduate visa, in particular, was reported to have the most widespread impact.

Announced in May 2025 by the UK government, the visa route duration will be shortened from 2 years to 18 months from 1 January 2027. Graduates from “high-compliance universities with strong labour market outcomes” will still be eligible for the full 2-year duration, as revealed in the Budget last month.

Three-quarters of business school deans said the reduction had a negative impact in 2025/26, with 82% expecting this to continue this academic year. Some 39% of schools see the visa as critically important to their ability to recruit international students.

The tightening of Basic Compliance Assessment (BCA) metrics has also had a substantial impact on enrolment numbers, with 60% of respondents noting a negative impact in 2025/26, rising to 74% for 2026/27.

Recruitment is expected to be harmed further if and when the government’s international student levy comes into force, with 71% predicting a negative impact.

Business schools are becoming less optimistic about the year ahead, with 60% expecting January 2027 enrolments to be lower year-on-year than last January. This is measured against last year’s survey, when 35% of schools expected January 2026 enrolments to increase and only 13% expected a decrease.

Falling enrolments come as business school finances are already strained. Almost half of responding deans reported a decrease in income for 2025/26, with three in five expecting their income to decline again in the current financial year.

This is a sharp contrast to last year’s survey, when 58% of schools expected their income to increase and only 21% anticipated a decline.

The financial strain also has knock-on effects for parent institutions. On average, responding business schools contributed 56% of their net income to their parent institutions in 2025/26. Half of respondents also said the most common request from financially challenged universities was for business schools to expand their international operations.

“Business schools are important anchor institutions in their local economies, delivering good growth in every postcode. That role is now being severely undermined,” said Robinson.

title: How Higher Ed Institutions Are Using Vibe Coding To Solve Problems
summary:
Many colleges and universities rely on custom software to address unique campus workflows or data privacy needs. Because of limited IT resources, relatively few have historically opted to build those applications on their own.
Now some are predicting that’s about to change as “vibe coding” within higher ed moves from niche to mainstream. The software development method entails describing an app in plain language and letting an AI assistant generate the code. The approach isn’t foolproof, those with experience say. But with practice and attention to data governance and security, it can be an…
full_text:
Practice and Patience Lead to Success at Emerson College

At Emerson, Basgen’s team has used vibe coding in Claude to develop nearly two dozen apps in-house.

“When the institution comes to us with a challenge,” he says, “the first thing I think about now is whether we can use AI to solve it.” The answer depends on the confidentiality of the data they’d need to make any solution functional, and it hinges on the hypothetical software’s overall importance to the college. “Anything highly complex, we’re not going to do it; if it’s available commercially, we’ll go with that instead.”

One recent problem that did meet the team’s requirements was Emerson’s need for a more effective way to manage hundreds of test cases during a student information system implementation. Normally, Basgen explains, with many people testing, they’d use spreadsheets and pivot tables to track the results.

DISCOVER: Customized software solutions help universities meet institutional goals.

“We were like, ‘Wouldn’t it be nice if we just made a simple web app so that everybody could access everything easily?’” Leveraging what he describes as their vibe-coding infrastructure — a standardized development environment created in Claude — they quickly built a solution that fit the bill. “We did it in almost no time at all, and it’s substantially better in terms of insights and tracking than the traditional implementation process.”

Other recent vibe-coded successes for the team include a security review app that helps staff understand Workday access configurations and troubleshoot missing permissions, and a department budget tracking app that integrates with financial data through Snowflake.

When Basgen and his colleagues first experimented with vibe coding in the fall of 2025, they found the technology difficult to work with and prone to making mistakes. Through trial and error, they eventually got up to speed, and now they have a repeatable process spanning everything from change control to code audits and security risk assessments.

“The No. 1 thing was getting started,” Basgen says. “After that, it was just persistence, patience and vision.”

READ MORE: A cyber resilience program should examine possible risk.

Vibe Coding at the University of Montana

Another IT leader who’s bullish about vibe coding is the University of Montana’s Zach Rossmiller, associate vice president and CIO. For the past several months, Rossmiller says, UM IT has hosted weekly “Vibe Fridays” to give campus employees dedicated time to explore how vibe coding might benefit them. They discuss their biggest challenges, test potential solutions, and for staff who don’t know where to start, his team provides guidance and encourages experimentation. “We’re trying to show them the possibilities,” he explains. “Like, here’s this AI tool, see what you can do.”

His team recently helped the UM Summer office use vibe coding to build a dashboard to analyze enrollment and estimate which courses might generate revenue versus costing the campus money. And for their own use, IT created a new systems status page after finding that a commercial product designed for that purpose included licensing restrictions that severely limited its utility. “After a couple hours, we had a prototype up and running that did what we needed it to do,” Rossmiller says.

Like Basgen, Rossmiller stresses the importance of treating vibe coded projects the same as any software requisition. Before they moved their status page app into production, for example, they put it through a battery of tests, including rigorous scanning and vulnerability assessments. And for any potential project that relies on access to the university’s data, “the first thing we’re going to do is talk to the data steward,” he says.

UP NEXT: Building an AI program requires a solid data strategy.

The way he sees it, Rossmiller adds, AI can produce a functioning app, but it can’t guarantee that software is going to be secure, accessible and maintainable.

“We’re very cautious with what we do and how we do it,” he says. “For us, that’s the only way to put vibe coding to work.”

title: What Sets Texas’s Elite Colleges Apart
summary: Undergraduate Study The rankings are based on an editorial, qualitative index that weighs first and foremost documented academic distinction, then research or creative work, then undergraduate opportunities, and, lastly, impact and scope beyond a narrow local mission. “Elite” means academic distinction. Elite does not imply that the schools are all equally selective (or that acceptance […]
full_text:
The rankings are based on an editorial, qualitative index that weighs first and foremost documented academic distinction, then research or creative work, then undergraduate opportunities, and, lastly, impact and scope beyond a narrow local mission.

“Elite” means academic distinction. Elite does not imply that the schools are all equally selective (or that acceptance rates are a ranking factor).

This is not an official ranking.

Texas has small colleges and big universities. Some schools are known for their research, others for their liberal arts curricula, and still others for tight-knit communities that thrive on a common curriculum.

Research-heavy universities are given a slight edge at the top of the list, but smaller schools make the list for their focused academic strengths. Texas’ universities are ranked by the institution or campus noted. Check out each school’s website for more information about costs, support services, and individual programs.

15

St. Edward’s University

Connects Personalized Study With Its Austin Setting

Founded by the Congregation of Holy Cross, St. Edward’s University emphasizes personalized education and learning through experience.1

For students interested in experiential learning opportunities such as internships and research, St. Edward’s offers several routes since many of these opportunities are incorporated into the undergraduate program.2 If you’re interested in a college where you can apply what you learn in the classroom to real-life settings (ideally, within your intended major!), St. Edward’s University could be an option for you.

St. Edward’s is a private school in Austin, TX.

The intimate setting and emphasis on close relationships between students and faculty may be an advantage for students who want a highly involved college experience. However, the effectiveness of the hands-on opportunities and feedback offered at St. Edward’s University will depend heavily on the student’s individual needs, goals, and fit with the school.

Before applying to St. Edward’s, interested students should carefully consider major and program requirements, hands-on learning opportunities, and the cost of attending after financial aid to determine whether St. Edward’s is the right school for them.

14

Austin College

Builds Academic Exploration Into JanTerm

Not ready to commit to a specific career track or college major?

Consider a college that incorporates exploration into its academic calendar. Austin College, for example, follows a liberal arts approach to higher education, placing greater emphasis on a well-rounded education, including rigorous writing and speaking courses, foreign language study, and real-world application, than narrow specialization.3

This makes it a good fit for students who are interested in a wide range of topics and want to see how different areas connect before committing to a particular area of study.

One element of its curriculum that supports exploration is JanTerm, a special session in January during which students enroll in just one intensive course.4 JanTerm courses often focus on subject matter that isn’t typically explored during a more traditional semester format and may take place on or off campus, through travel, career exploration, or other experiential opportunities.

However, it’s important for potential AC students to learn more about exactly what kinds of JanTerm courses are offered, how students choose their JanTerm course, and whether off-campus opportunities include additional travel expenses. While JanTerm can add an intriguing line to a college transcript, the key to getting the most out of this unique academic offering is to select a JanTerm that aligns with your broader educational goals.

13

University of Dallas

Requires a Shared Core of Major Texts and Ideas

The University of Dallas ranks in part because of its distinctive approach to the curriculum, built around a demanding common core of major texts and ideas from the Western tradition.5

Dallas’s common core is an attempt to create a shared curriculum concerned with fundamental questions about who we are as human beings, about nature and God. Dallas’s Rome experience also tries to make study abroad an integral part of the academic program instead of a respite from it: literature, history, theology, philosophy, art, and architecture are all studied in Rome itself.6

The University of Dallas may appeal to students who want a demanding common core and a clearly defined approach to a liberal-arts education, and who will thrive in the program as it is.

The same features will be drawbacks for others. Prospective students should look through the required reading list and other requirements to see whether Dallas’s common core is the kind they’re interested in, and also look into what Rome involves: who can go, when, and at what cost.

12

Southwestern University

Teaches Students to Connect Ideas Across Subjects

Southwestern University’s approach begins with the liberal arts core curriculum’s introductory Paideia Seminar.

This experience is then supplemented with interdisciplinary work within each student’s major and culminates with a capstone project.8 How does the evidence from scientists, the work of ethicists, and the understanding of the behavior of citizens and elected officials come together to provide insight and possible solutions to environmental problems?

We ranked research universities higher than Southwestern University not because of a lack of ambition at SU, but because the emphasis is different at research universities.

Before applying to Southwestern University, prospective students should ask about the ways in which interdisciplinary study occurs within their intended majors, and what makes a good capstone project. A flexible liberal arts education7 is best when students can explain how all of the pieces fit together and precisely what their capstone project represents.

11

University of Texas at Arlington

Offers Research and Professional Study in North Texas

The University of Texas at Arlington is a public research university,9 where undergraduates can explore research, professional internships and leadership opportunities.

When considering colleges and universities, don’t rely on reputation alone. For example, UTA has a reputation for offering research opportunities to its students and its breadth of academic offerings, rather than selectivity.

The breadth of academic programs offered can be a major plus for students whose interests cross subject areas, or for students who aren’t certain what major they want to declare.

UTA organizes its academic offerings into schools and colleges, and you can learn more about the academic programs each unit offers.10 As with any large institution, it’s important to understand which degree requirements are university-wide and which are specific to a particular degree or major.

Learn more about academic progression requirements to see what kinds of undergraduate research opportunities may be available to you during your time at UTA. When it comes down to it, what matters most is the educational path you’ll pursue. A big university with lots of options isn’t necessarily better than a smaller one, because it’s what you do with those options that matters.

10

Texas Tech University

Combines a Research Mission With Broad Program Choice

Texas Tech is a large public research university known for combining strong teaching with active research.11

The list of programs at Texas Tech separates graduate/professional and undergraduate programs,12 as this can significantly affect your experience. Having a top law or medical school does not necessarily mean that the freshman experience is just as strong.

If you’re unsure where to begin, narrow your list down according to the degree program you’re interested in, and then do some additional research on that program’s strengths, hands-on opportunities, research access, advising, and so on.

If you’re seeking a specialized technical or professional program, Texas Tech might be a better value for you than a smaller, less comprehensive school ranked higher than Texas Tech. Consider the resources Texas Tech offers in your area of interest in addition to the school’s comprehensive academic programs, and you’ll find that Texas Tech can be a good fit for you.

9

University of Texas at Dallas

Connects Design Projects With Industry Clients

The UTDesign program at UT Dallas is an example of undergraduate work that is grounded in real-world industry collaboration.13

Through UTDesign, students in the engineering and computer science disciplines work on projects designed to develop skills in project management, teamwork, and applying design knowledge to real problems.14 Each of these skills is individually challenging, but combining them all makes a project more difficult because solutions must not only be technically feasible, but also well-organized and understandable.

These projects give students important practice tying together all of these crucial elements.

That said, it’s important to keep in mind that this program is specific to the engineering and computer science disciplines – students in other fields may or may not have similar capstone experiences. It’s important to research exactly what type of capstone project (if any) your potential major has, as well as how those projects are evaluated.

An effective graduate not only knows how to do something, but can explain their decisions.

8

University of Houston

Adds an Honors Core to a Large Research University

Applying to the Honors College at a large, public research university may offer several advantages.

At Texas Christian University, your experience is centered on your academic interests, and you’ll likely combine a robust undergraduate education with a major in one of TCU’s many schools and colleges.

A TCU degree has a lot to offer, but the experience at this university will ultimately depend on finding the right fit for you and having access to TCU’s many resources and programs.

Connects a Christian Mission With Research

Baylor University is a private Christian university with a focus on high-level research.19

When deciding whether to apply to Baylor, compare departments, consider what you want your college experience to be, and calculate the final cost. Baylor University is known for its strong research programs, but student learning doesn’t end after stepping away from a computer or leaving the lab.

The University emphasizes teaching and faculty mentorship and encourages learning experiences outside of the traditional classroom such as hands-on research projects and other guided learning experiences.20

For students who would feel at home in such an environment, Baylor’s combination of a broad range of academic programs with an emphasis on research could be a great fit.

Supports Summer Research With Faculty Mentors

Trinity University combines breadth-focused academics and research funding opportunities.

Prospective students could include Trinity on their list of schools to consider, especially if they are also looking at research universities. Located in Dallas, Tex., Southern Methodist University benefits from its close ties to a thriving metropolis that offers cultural and professional networking opportunities, and from which it also draws collaborators.23

Success here comes from the connections students make with faculty and other students, and the persistence it takes to cultivate those relationships. The ranking rewards all of that, not just the name on the door. Prospective students should look into the individual schools, see what creative and research opportunities are available and how internships and other experiential learning opportunities fit into the academic calendar.

They should also compare financial aid offers.

A broad private university with connections to a major city is attractive in many ways, but it makes the most sense for students who feel those resources, activities and opportunities are aligned with their interests and preparation.

Texas A&M’s mission also emphasizes teaching, service and leadership.25

Students benefit from this comprehensive approach as they gain a well-rounded education and develop many different skills. There’s a lot to like about Texas A&M, but what sets it apart from other top research schools is its strong focus on undergraduate education.

Texas A&M students can pursue in-depth, discipline-specific knowledge while taking advantage of the resources available at a massive research institution.

Different programs have different admissions requirements. Some majors are more selective than others, and the school experience can vary by campus location.26

Be sure to check admission and progression requirements, program-specific admissions information and campus location information so you know exactly what resources will be available to you if you attend Texas A&M. Combines Academic Breadth With Research Across Fields

While Texas has more than its share of top private universities and focused schools, UT Austin’s research reach and academic breadth make it a strong contender as a well-rounded school.

That breadth, and an emphasis on collaboration, dialogue and learning both in and out of the classroom, sets UT Austin’s academics apart. But be aware, acceptance into UT Austin does not necessarily equate to acceptance into your desired program.

Be sure to review the most recent admissions requirements and criteria to understand what the university is looking for in candidates.

However, the size of the university means that students have many resources to help them adjust to life on a large campus. UT Austin’s programs and research stretch far and wide, literally.

Its contributions to knowledge reach far outside the confines of any single discipline, department or even school.27 You can immerse yourself in your area of study, but never have to sacrifice a chat over coffee with someone pursuing a very different academic interest. While impressive research output doesn’t always translate to accessible research opportunities for undergrads, access varies by program.

All told, Rice University proves that a research university doesn’t have to be massive in order to offer intellectual breadth.

summary: Prime aperture degli istituti sul rinnovo, ma pesa il contesto molto incerto sia per le conseguenze della manovra di bilancio che per le operazioni straordinarie
full_text:
La tassa sugli extraprofitti delle banche fa irruzione al tavolo Abi dove il Comitato affari sindacali e del lavoro dell’associazione, guidato da Ilaria Maria Dalla Riva e i sindacati (Fabi, First, Fisac, Uilca e Unisin) stanno discutendo il rinnovo del contratto che riguarda oltre 260mila lavoratori bancari ed è scaduto lo scorso marzo. Il segretario generale della Fabi, Lando Maria Sileoni, parla di prime aperture, ma sull’andamento della trattativa pesa la forte incertezza che si registra su almeno due fronti: il primo è la manovra di bilancio che potrebbe sottrarre molte risorse alle banche, il secondo sono le operazioni straordinarie. In assenza di un quadro certo sembra difficile che la trattativa possa decollare.

Per Sileoni, «per arrivare alla conclusione del rinnovo del contratto nazionale è necessario che il Casl dell’Abi si prenda il mandato per affrontare e definire tutte le questioni ancora aperte».

Certamente va detto che per una compiuta valutazione complessiva della piattaforma, compresa quindi la parte economica su cui i sindacati chiedono 518 euro di aumento a regime per il livello medio di riferimento, occorre avere piena contezza di tutti gli elementi di contesto sul settore del credito, per evidenti ragioni di visione d’insieme. Il Casl di Abi sta continuando ad approfondire tutti i punti della piattaforma. Il confronto proseguirà speditamente, il prossimo incontro è previsto già per il 19 novembre. «I tempi di chiusura del contratto nazionale di lavoro sono importanti - evidenzia Sileoni - ma conta soprattutto come si arriva alla firma e quali risultati si riescono a ottenere per le lavoratrici e i lavoratori bancari».

Nel corso dell’incontro sono stati affrontati diversi temi. Quello all’ordine del giorno era il Fondo per l’occupazione che viene finanziato dai lavoratori e dalle banche e che è stato creato per incentivare le nuove assunzioni di giovani: dalla sua nascita ad oggi ha favorito l’ingresso in banca di oltre 40mila giovani. Sul Foc, Sileoni ha chiaramente spiegato che i sindacati non sono disponibili «a snaturare uno strumento nato per sostenere l’occupazione, trasferendo sul Fondo costi che spettano ai gruppi bancari. Siamo invece pronti a ragionare su un protocollo più ampio per l’occupazione, all’interno di un progetto organico e condiviso. Occorre quindi verificare fino in fondo tutte le disponibilità dell’Abi per valutare complessivamente tutti gli argomenti».

Quanto agli altri temi, sulle operazioni straordinarie, Riccardo Colombani, numero uno della First Cisl, ha evidenziato che «non dobbiamo dimenticare che sono poco meno di 200mila i bancari che saranno coinvolti nelle operazioni di ristrutturazione e riorganizzazione del risiko bancario: è giusto dare loro risposte in tempi stretti ed eliminare ogni incertezza. Dal prossimo incontro, in programma il 19 novembre, ci aspettiamo quindi un’accelerazione. In quella sede il Casl si è impegnato a discutere del Protocollo per l’occupazione, un passo avanti da valutare nei contenuti, vista l’esigenza di gestire le trasformazioni che attraversano il settore e governare l’utilizzo delle nuove tecnologie». Sulla tassa sugli extraprofitti, Colombani aggiunge che «dalla fine del 2022 fino ad oggi si è assistito ad una divaricazione fortissima dei benefici tra gli azionisti e i lavoratori, a tutto vantaggio dei primi, che incamerano la parte più cospicua dei proventi operativi. Abi giustifica il suo ritardo con l’introduzione da parte del governo di un nuovo contributo sulle banche nella legge di bilancio. Ciò non è rispettoso delle lavoratrici e dei lavoratori che sono stati decisivi per raggiungere i risultati record degli ultimi anni, tanto più ora che l’inflazione torna a crescere ed erode il potere d’acquisto delle retribuzioni».
